source.title: Neural Scaling Universality: If Exponents Are Fixed, Time to Understand Coefficients

record.tranche_reason: The paper re-fits held-out loss data from existing model families to fixed- and free-exponent scaling forms and analyzes compute-optimal points. This is a conceptual test of scaling behavior, not a reproduction of the original studies' training experiments.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own fits and analyses of Pythia, reconstructed Chinchilla, and Farseer loss data. Cited results from other work—including the original Kaplan and Hoffmann findings—are not recorded as rows. Downstream-task claims and claims about other modalities are discussed or cited, not tested here.
record.test_reason: The study evaluates scaling forms through new held-out Pythia evaluations and reanalysis of Chinchilla and Farseer loss data. It tests loss scaling, compute allocation, modeled shape sensitivity, and selected aspects of fit dependence. It does not perform a small-to-large extrapolation test.
record.authors_conclusion: The record captures the authors' position, but should state its provisional status: they propose a universality hypothesis with fixed asymptotic exponents and argue that coefficients govern practical shape and allocation choices. Their selected-data fits are consistent with this framework; they explicitly call for further verification and acknowledge other scaling regimes. They do not establish universality through controlled changes to architecture or data.
record.recipe_differences: Reanalysis and nonlinear fitting of existing model-family loss data, with fixed- and free-exponent fits and isoFLOP analysis; it does not reproduce the original training experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: The asymptotic fit depends on excluding insufficiently trained Chinchilla points and high-loss Farseer runs. Derived coefficients and optimal token-to-parameter ratios vary across model families.

fits_no_version.finding: Pythia held-out loss follows a power law in learning-rate-integrated dynamic time, with representative free exponents 0.31–0.37.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Held-out language-model loss follows a power law in integrated optimization time after warmup.

fits_no_version.finding: Joint fits decompose saturation or total loss into inverse-width and inverse-depth contributions; Pythia evidence is weaker because of its limited size range.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In an asymptotic additive loss model, representation and transformation contributions scale approximately inversely with width and depth.

record.problems: The paper reanalyzes existing or reconstructed data rather than running controlled new training experiments. Some early or high-loss points are excluded to obtain asymptotic fits; the authors note that Pythia provides a limited size range for width and depth evidence. The paper reports that coefficients and derived ratios vary across families.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant own-result rows omitted. Cited findings from earlier papers and downstream-task or modality claims without new measurements are excluded.

untested.parts: The full several-orders-of-magnitude, non-bottleneck claim is not independently established for every scaling axis and family. Pythia's temporal result uses dynamic time, and its width/depth components do not directly test parameter-count scaling.
No fit restricted to small runs is evaluated against held-out runs orders of magnitude larger.

No direct experimental search validates the fitted optima, no controlled comparison resolves Kaplan versus Hoffmann allocation prescriptions, and stability beyond the analyzed compute ranges is untested.
Independent fixed-parameter architecture sweeps, shapes far from the modeled optimum, and architectural details beyond depth/width are untested.
Other modalities, repeated-data training, fine-tuning, and transfer are discussed or proposed without relevant new results.
No downstream performance or downstream prediction measurements are reported.

Controlled sensitivity of exponents to parameter counting, schedules, data, and fitting methods is untested. The study does not quantitatively explain published disagreements or causally attribute cross-family allocation differences.

missing.what: Chinchilla's direct parameter-count and dataset-size fit using the optimal-shape form agrees with one-third scaling on 235 retained points. Table 3 reports cD = 1076 ± 8, cN = 374 ± 2, and L0 = 1.762 ± 0.003.

Alternative Chinchilla parameterizations produce different derived allocation constants: the separate width/depth fit gives D/N = 36.4 ± 2.1, whereas applying Equation (9) to Table 3 gives (1076/374)^3 ≈ 23.8. The latter is calculated from the reported coefficients; its uncertainty is not supplied.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not either original source, although much of its evidence reuses original Chinchilla experiments. No V1 challenge or scope limitation is assigned solely because insufficiently trained points depart from the asymptotic law: those points do not establish failure under V1's stated non-bottleneck conditions. Fixed-exponent profile fitting and fitted component subtraction make several results conditional consistency checks rather than independent validations.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test every scaling regime, model family, or range of training conditions; its claims are limited to the analyzed data and asymptotic fits.
Does not fit only small runs and then evaluate predictions against runs orders of magnitude larger.
Tests compute-optimal scaling on Chinchilla and Farseer data, not all compute budgets or training setups.
Tests a modeled range of aspect ratios for Chinchilla; does not independently vary every architectural detail at fixed parameter count.
No experiments on other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer.
Does not evaluate downstream-task performance or its predictability from scale or pretraining loss.

Does not systematically vary fitting procedures to quantify how much exponents change; it reports sensitivity to asymptotic-data selection and differences in derived optimal ratios across model families.

rows.subject: Pythia models (eight models; 70M, 160M, 410M, 1B, 1.4B, 2.8B, 6.9B, and 12B)
rows.operation_detail: Fit held-out loss against dynamic time with the time exponent fixed at 1/3; also fit a free exponent for four representative models.
rows.measure: Held-out cross-entropy loss versus dynamic time
rows.value: Training loss is described as well fit by one-third scaling; free-fit exponents for 70M, 410M, 2.8B, and 12B are in [0.31, 0.37].
rows.note: The reported fit is across the Pythia models; the free-exponent range is for four representative models.
rows.check: The measured power law is in learning-rate-integrated dynamic time, rather than parameters, tokens, or compute as named in V1. Its reported exponent range is correct, but it does not establish the corresponding raw-token or compute exponent. The fit also excludes the first one or two checkpoints.

rows.subject: Pythia models (six largest models, 410M–12B)
rows.operation_detail: Fit saturation loss to inverse width plus inverse depth and an irreducible-loss term.

conditions.value: Joint fit of six largest models; two smallest excluded

rows.value: The saturation loss is described as well described by inverse-width and inverse-depth scaling once width and depth are large enough; the width evidence is described as less strongly conclusive because the suite spans a limited size range.
rows.note: The paper jointly fits width and depth contributions and cautions that the Pythia size range gives weaker evidence for these than for time scaling.
rows.check: This is an inverse-width component fitted jointly with depth, rather than a direct parameter-count scaling result or a comparison of shapes at fixed parameter count. Limited evidence is not itself an incomplete effect.

rows.subject: Chinchilla models
rows.operation_detail: Jointly fit reconstructed loss data to dataset-size, width, and depth scaling terms with fixed exponents; also fit free exponents.

conditions.value: 245 reconstructed data points; 10 smallest-dataset-size points excluded, leaving 235

rows.measure: Held-out loss versus training dataset size
rows.value: The free-fit dataset exponent is 0.34 ± 0.01; the authors state that the dataset-size scaling is well supported on the retained data.
rows.note: The fitted dataset-size term is reported as a power law on the selected asymptotic subset.
rows.check: The reported dataset exponent supports power-law loss on the retained subset. One exponent estimate alone does not demonstrate V7's dependence on setup or fitting choices.

rows.subject: Chinchilla models
rows.operation_detail: Jointly fit reconstructed loss data to dataset-size, width, and depth scaling terms with fixed exponents; also fit free exponents.
rows.value: The free-fit width exponent is 0.87 ± 0.06; the authors describe the result as broadly consistent with 1 and state that the width scaling is supported.
rows.note: The paper reports this free-exponent result alongside the jointly fitted fixed-exponent formula.
rows.check: The row measures a fitted width component, not loss against parameter count or shape variation at fixed parameter count. The reported exponent is correct.

rows.operation_detail: Jointly fit reconstructed loss data to dataset-size, width, and depth scaling terms with fixed exponents; also fit free exponents.
rows.value: The free-fit depth exponent is 0.97 ± 0.20; the authors describe the result as broadly consistent with 1 and state that the depth scaling is supported.
rows.note: The paper reports this free-exponent result alongside the jointly fitted fixed-exponent formula.
rows.check: The row measures a fitted depth component, not loss against parameter count or shape variation at fixed parameter count. The reported exponent is correct.

rows.subject: Chinchilla models
rows.operation_detail: Compared early-training points with the fitted asymptotic scaling regime.
rows.measure: Whether early-training loss points follow the asymptotic power law
rows.baseline: Asymptotic scaling fit on retained points
rows.value: The excluded points are stated not to follow the asymptotic scaling because training is insufficient and D ∝ τ breaks down.
rows.note: The departure is attributed to insufficient training, not to a failure of the asymptotic fit on the retained data.
rows.check: The stated departure from a single asymptotic law bears on V7. These insufficiently trained points do not establish failure within V1's non-bottleneck regime. The cutoff was selected by scanning removals and minimizing fitted-parameter uncertainty.

rows.subject: Farseer models
rows.operation_detail: Fit loss against model size with a fixed one-third exponent and a free-exponent form.

conditions.value: 404 loss points; 80 highest-loss points excluded, leaving 324

rows.value: The free-fit model-size exponent is 0.30 ± 0.01, described as broadly consistent with 1/3; the fixed-exponent fit is reported as agreeing well.
rows.note: Farseer has m ∝ ℓ, so separate width and depth coefficients cannot be identified; the paper fits the combined model-size term.
rows.check: The free exponent supports power-law parameter scaling on the retained subset. Its difference from exactly one-third does not contradict V1, which specifies no particular exponent, or independently demonstrate V7.

rows.subject: Farseer models
rows.operation_detail: Fit loss against training dataset size with a fixed one-third exponent and a free-exponent form.

conditions.value: 404 loss points; 80 highest-loss points excluded, leaving 324

rows.value: The free-fit dataset-size exponent is 0.349 ± 0.009, described as broadly consistent with 1/3; the fixed-exponent fit is reported as agreeing well.
rows.note: The reported fits use the retained lower-loss data points.
rows.check: The free exponent supports power-law dataset scaling on the retained subset. This single fit does not independently demonstrate setup or fitting dependence.

rows.subject: Farseer models
rows.operation_detail: Compared highest-loss points with the fitted asymptotic model-size and dataset-size scaling form.
rows.measure: Whether high-loss runs follow the asymptotic power law
rows.baseline: Asymptotic scaling fit on retained points
rows.value: The excluded highest-loss points are stated to be under-trained runs where the asymptotic power law does not yet apply.
rows.note: The paper selects an asymptotic subset by excluding high-loss runs.
rows.check: The authors explicitly identify a regime outside the asymptotic law. This supports V7's regime qualification; under-trained runs do not establish failure within V1's non-bottleneck regime. The exclusion count was selected by minimizing fitted-parameter uncertainty.

rows.subject: Chinchilla models
rows.operation_detail: Compared modeled loss across aspect ratios at fixed parameter count near the optimal shape.

conditions.value: Compute-optimal point with the same N

rows.measure: Increase in reducible loss L − L0 relative to the optimum
